CRASH RECOVERY RECIPE — PROVEN 2026-07-23 when the Claude Code host process exited with 6 workers mid-run. Follow in this order; the order is the whole point.

THE ONE FACT THAT DECIDES EVERYTHING: workers have died two entirely different ways in one session — a stream watchdog killing them after a long silent stretch, and the host process exiting. In BOTH cases the line between "fully recovered" and "lost" was exactly: WAS IT PUSHED? Commits on a worker branch survive anything. Uncommitted files survive only as long as nobody reaps the worktree.

STEP 1 — GROUND TRUTH, before touching anything. For each worktree, git-only (never a filesystem walk):
  git -C <wt> rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD     # unpushed commits
  git -C <wt> status --porcelain | grep -v .beads    # uncommitted WIP
  git ls-remote --heads origin <branch> | wc -l      # is the branch on origin at all
Classify: branch-on-origin = safe. Commits-but-no-remote = AT RISK. Zero-commits-plus-dirty-plus-no-remote = MOST at risk.

STEP 2 — MERGE ANY GREEN PR FIRST. A PR that was green when the process died is free progress and it unblocks whatever was sequenced behind it.

STEP 3 — PUSH THE COMMITTED-BUT-UNPUSHED WORK YOURSELF. This is pure durability and carries no judgement risk: the commits already exist, you are only making them survivable. Do NOT open a PR from them.

⚠️ STEP 4 — DO NOT COMMIT A WORKER UNCOMMITTED WIP YOURSELF. Tell the worker to do it. There is a recorded incident in this project where a mayor committed a worker partial work as a recovery PR and merged an incomplete state that broke main. Uncommitted files are mid-edit by definition; only the worker knows whether they form a coherent commit. The mayor pushes COMMITS, never creates them from someone else WIP.

STEP 5 — RESUME EVERY WORKER, with a message tailored to ITS state, leading with durability:
  - Say plainly it was not stopped for cause and its work is safe — a worker that thinks it failed behaves worse.
  - For the most-at-risk one, make the FIRST instruction "commit what you have (even as a WIP commit) and push, BEFORE rebasing, BEFORE gates, BEFORE anything."
  - Tell it exactly what landed on main while it was gone, and whether its rebase is EXPECTED (sequenced deliberately) rather than a surprise to investigate.
  - Re-state only the must-survive laws and traps specific to that worker — not the whole original brief.
THIS WORKED, MEASURED: the worst-off worker went from 0 commits / 12 uncommitted files / no remote branch to 3 commits pushed on its first resumed turn.

STEP 6 — clear any stale .git/index.lock left by the abrupt exit, then re-export beads FROM DOLT (never git checkout over them) and checkpoint.

PREVENTION, now standard in every dispatch brief and worth more than the recipe: "COMMIT AND PUSH AS YOU GO — not at the end", stated WITH the reason (two mechanisms have killed workers; incremental pushing is the only defence against both). Also: a bigger in-flight bubble is a proportionally bigger crash surface — saturation is right, but keep it within what one recovery pass can handle.

A TEST FIXTURE CAN MAKE AN ABSENCE ASSERTION UNSATISFIABLE — the inverse false green. Found by the rf2-vxgfnd.299 worker (#6416) on 2026-07-19.

THE CASE: an elision gate asserted a sentinel ABSENT from an :advanced production bundle. After the fix landed, the sentinel STAYED PINNED AT 2. The gated library call HAD correctly folded to nil — but the FIXTURE own probe, `(:build-digest (client/descriptor ::probe))`, kept the keyword alive in the bundle as Wk.g(null). The assertion was measuring THE FIXTURE, NOT THE LIBRARY, and could never pass however correct the fix. Fixed by having the fixture export the whole descriptor via clj->js instead of destructuring the sentinel key.

WHY THIS IS ITS OWN SPECIES: every other false green this session was a check THAT COULD NOT FAIL. This is a check THAT COULD NOT SUCCEED. Both are the same underlying error — an assertion decoupled from the thing it names — but the failure mode is inverted, and the tell is different: a permanently-red arm that survives a correct fix is as suspicious as a permanently-green one. If a fix is right and the arm still reds, SUSPECT THE HARNESS BEFORE RE-FIXING THE CODE.
RULE FOR ANY ABSENCE ASSERTION: check whether the TEST CODE ITSELF references the symbol being asserted absent. A probe that names the thing it is proving gone will root it.

RELATED, AND THE RIGHT SHAPE FOR A NON-VACUITY FLOOR (same PR): the floor must witness that THE NAMESPACE UNDER TEST IS ACTUALLY IN THE SCANNED ARTIFACT, otherwise an absence is attributable to the namespace having been dropped entirely rather than to the gate. #6416 floor is a STRING LITERAL (Closure never rewrites them — the property that killed the function-name oracle), UNGATED, ROOTED FROM init, and reached through an UNGATED CLIENT REGISTRY READ. Verified discriminating on the same bundle with the same grep: floor at 1 while a known-absent sentinel reads 0.

WHEN A NEW TEST CAUSES WIDESPREAD FAILURES IN UNRELATED SUITES, BASELINE MAIN BEFORE DIAGNOSING. Learned 2026-07-24 by the bench-evidence worker, which caught it on itself.

THE INCIDENT: its first B1 draft used Promise.all over two act() mounts and LEAKED A LIVE ROOT on rejection. That cascaded into 98 FAILURES ACROSS UNRELATED SUITES plus a suite-wide timeout — failures in pilot_field and pilot_overlay, which its change had nothing to do with. It ran the suite with its own new file REMOVED, proved main was green (642 tests, 0 failures), and only then knew the fault was entirely its own.

⚠️ WITHOUT THAT BASELINE IT WOULD HAVE CHASED PHANTOM REGRESSIONS in other people work — and in a repo with several workers in flight, the natural (wrong) conclusion is "someone else broke main".

THE RULE: a broad, cross-suite failure after a LOCAL change is almost always YOUR change leaking shared state, not a real regression elsewhere. Before diagnosing anything: remove your new file (or stash-free equivalent: check out the pre-change tree) and re-run. If main is green, the fault is yours and the blast radius is a CONTAMINATION signal, not a map of what is broken.

THE SPECIFIC HAZARD, worth knowing on its own: in a shared-process test bundle, a LEAKED REACT ROOT contaminates every later suite. Promise.all over concurrent mounts is the classic way to leak one — on rejection the other mount is never released. Fix shape: await each mount IN TURN, disambiguate them, and release in a `finally`. This is the same family as the process-global tables that must be reset between suites; anything holding a live handle across a test boundary poisons alphabetical successors.

RELATED FINDING FROM THE SAME WORKER: THE BROWSER LANE DISCARDS CONSOLE OUTPUT ON SUCCESS. Published evidence records are only captured under RF2_VERBOSE_TESTS=1. So a test that intends to inspect emitted evidence sees nothing on a passing run unless that flag is set — another way an assertion can be measuring an empty stream.

GATE LOGS MUST NOT GO TO /tmp UNDER MULTI-AGENT LOAD — /tmp is SHARED across concurrently running worker agents on this box, so one worker gate log silently OVERWRITES another. Found 2026-07-24 by the rf2-drpa3.112 SSR worker, which nearly shipped a false green.

THE MECHANISM: worker A runs "npm run test:browser > /tmp/gate-browser.log 2>&1". Worker B, running concurrently in a DIFFERENT worktree, writes the same path. A then reads a log that is really B run. In the observed case the log EXIT=0 and reported "0 failures" — every number looked right. The ONLY tell was the shadow-cljs banner naming the WRONG worktree (pilot-react-interop-46 instead of the reader own).

WHY THIS IS NASTY: it defeats the standard exit-code discipline. The capture-to-a-file-and-echo-the-exit-code rule was adopted precisely because piping into tail/grep discards the runner exit status. But if the FILE ITSELF belongs to another agent, the captured exit code is ALSO another agent — a correct technique reading the wrong evidence. Both the summary AND the exit code agree, and both are about someone else run.

THE FIX, now standard in every dispatch brief: write gate logs to the SESSION SCRATCHPAD or a worktree-local path, never a bare /tmp name. e.g.
  <gate> > "$WT/gate-<name>.log" 2>&1; echo "EXIT=$?"; tail -30 "$WT/gate-<name>.log"
And VERIFY OWNERSHIP: the shadow-cljs "config:" banner line names the worktree whose build ran. Grep it and confirm it is YOURS before believing any number in that file. That is the cheap proof.

MAYOR NOTE: my own standing gate-discipline boilerplate said "> /tmp/gate.log". That instruction is now known-unsafe whenever more than one worker runs at a time, which is the normal case at saturation. Update the boilerplate; do not keep handing workers a colliding path.

GENERAL FORM: this joins the roster of ways green has meant nothing-was-measured here. The others are about a check that could not fail; this one is about a check that MEASURED SOMEBODY ELSE. When an assertion rests on an artefact OUTSIDE your process (a shared temp file, a shared port, a shared cache), ask WHO ELSE CAN WRITE IT before trusting what you read.

FLAKE PROOF — a run count is not always the right evidence; sometimes a MARGIN is. I briefed rf2-ybqse to prove stability with 20+ consecutive runs. Its worker (2026-07-18) correctly pushed back: focused runs could not exercise that flake at all (the bug lived in the gap between namespace LOAD and render, which a focused run collapses), and full-suite runs cost ~4 min each. It ran 20 focused + 3 full and supplied the better proof — the measured margin between the fixture's :stale-at and the render-time clock: +30461ms pre-fix (29.5s of a 60s horizon already burned), -13700ms when deliberately shrunk to falsify (reproducing the reported failure string verbatim), +60000ms post-fix. At a constant 60000ms the failure is UNREACHABLE rather than merely unobserved. RULE FOR BRIEFS: ask for proof the failure is unreachable, and let the worker choose the instrument. Repeated green runs prove absence-of-observation; a margin, an invariant, or a falsification run can prove absence-of-possibility. Demanding N runs can also mislead — N greens on a test that structurally cannot fail in that mode is a false-green about a false-green. ALSO: this class of flake (wall-clock captured in a top-level def, compared against a render-time clock) is invisible in isolation and only appears when a bundle loads all namespaces before executing any.

Junction-rmdir trap (RECURRED 2x, 2026-06-10): a worktree's implementation/node_modules is often a JUNCTION to the mayor checkout's real node_modules (workers npm-install/junction it to run node gates). 'git worktree remove --force' on such a worktree DELETES THROUGH the junction into the mayor's REAL node_modules (emptying it to 0) UNLESS the junction link is removed FIRST. THE BREAKING BUG (hit twice): building the rmdir path via bash sed inside a nested powershell double-quoted string — e.g. cmd /c rmdir '$(echo $p|sed 's#/#\#g')' — the sed errors 'unterminated s command' (nested-quote mangling), rmdir gets a broken path + fails ('syntax of the command is incorrect'), the junction survives, and worktree-remove nukes the target. CORRECT junction removal (PowerShell-native, NO bash sed, NO backslash conversion): powershell -NoProfile -Command "$p='<FORWARD-slash path>'; $i=Get-Item $p -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; if($i -and $i.LinkType){ [System.IO.Directory]::Delete($p,$false) }; Test-Path $p"  — [System.IO.Directory]::Delete(path,$false) removes the reparse point WITHOUT recursing into the target; forward-slashes work fine in .NET; VERIFY Test-Path returns False BEFORE git worktree remove. BOTH /tmp AND THE SESSION SCRATCHPAD ARE SHARED ACROSS CONCURRENT AGENTS ON THIS HOST. Two independent workers hit this on 2026-07-24, in two different directories.

INSTANCE 1 — /tmp: a worker gate log written to /tmp/gate-browser.log was overwritten by ANOTHER worker run. It read EXIT=0 and "0 failures" — plausible numbers, wrong code. The only tell was the shadow-cljs "config:" banner naming a different worktree. This defeats the capture-and-echo-the-exit-code discipline, because the captured EXIT CODE belongs to the other run too.

INSTANCE 2 — THE SCRATCHPAD: the v/->react worker had its pr-body.md OVERWRITTEN by another worker mid-task. Caught before it did damage, but a PR body is exactly the kind of file you write once and read back later without re-checking.

THE RULE, now standard in every brief: write worker-owned files to a WORKTREE-LOCAL path, not /tmp and not a bare name in the shared scratchpad. If the scratchpad must be used, make the filename UNIQUE (include the branch or bead id). And VERIFY OWNERSHIP before believing any captured artefact — for a shadow-cljs run, the "config:" banner names the worktree whose build ran; grep it and confirm it is yours.

GENERAL FORM, which is why this outlives both instances: when an assertion or an artefact rests on something OUTSIDE your process — a shared temp directory, a shared port, a shared cache, a scratchpad — ask WHO ELSE CAN WRITE IT before trusting what you read back. A file you wrote is not necessarily the file you read. This is the same family as the console-shim trap (the observer sits below your runtime) and the attribute-order trap (the serialisation carries incidental detail) — in every case the thing being measured is not the thing you think you are measuring.

MAYOR NOTE: my own boilerplate said "> /tmp/gate.log" for a long stretch of dispatches. Saturating six workers on one machine makes shared-path collision the NORMAL case, not an edge case.

NEVER 'bd import' A JSONL YOU JUST REVERTED — IT CORRUPTS THE DOLT DB (root-caused 2026-07-25). The Dolt database is the SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH; .beads/issues.jsonl is a derived export. The mayor's conflict-reconcile procedure was: git checkout HEAD -- .beads (to unblock a pull) -> git pull --rebase -> rebase --skip -> bd import .beads/issues.jsonl -> bd export. The import step feeds the REVERTED (pre-close) file back INTO the database, resurrecting beads that were legitimately closed minutes earlier. Confirmed on rf2-a32r7: closed with a full reason, zero AUDIT-REOPEN notes, back to OPEN after one reconcile cycle. Also hit rf2-kqxe6.17 (twice), rf2-8ewl1, rf2-x4jda. CORRECT PROCEDURE — the file is downstream of the DB, data only ever flows DB -> file: (1) git checkout HEAD -- .beads  (2) git pull --ff-only  (3) bd export --all -o .beads/issues.jsonl  (4) guard wc -l >= 2000  (5) git add + commit + push. On a push rejection, repeat from (1) — NEVER 'bd import'. Import is ONLY for restoring a database that is itself lost or empty, never as a merge step. DIAGNOSTIC that distinguishes this from a genuine reviewer reopen: a real reopen carries a MERGED-PR AUDIT / AUDIT-REOPEN note naming an unmet defect at a code site; a procedure-revert has ZERO reopen notes and the bead simply reads open with its pre-close state. Grep the notes before re-closing.

TWO CLJS/CLOJURE TRAPS found by the rf2-ycz3k worker (#6415) WHILE building, not by a gate.

(1) NAMESPACE-CLOBBERING FACADE DEF. Naming a namespace re-frame.ssr.boundary and then exporting (def boundary ...) from the facade compiles to `re_frame.ssr.boundary = re_frame.ssr.boundary.boundary;` — THE ASSIGNMENT DESTROYS THE NAMESPACE OBJECT. Shipping bug, found only because the worker exercised the built artefact. RULE: never let a facade export share its bare name with a namespace segment under the same root. Fix structurally (rename the ns; keep the authoring name) rather than renaming the public verb.

(2) clojure.test HAS NO MAP FIXTURES — and the failure mode is a SILENT GREEN. A map is IFn, so `(use-fixtures :each {:before f :after g})` composes to a function that returns nil WITHOUT RUNNING THE TEST BODY. Output is "Ran 0 tests ... 0 failures", exit 0. The worker caught it ONLY because the suite count did not move off 456. RULE: use a plain fn fixture `(fn [t] (before) (t) (after))`. And this is the concrete reason every brief must demand a NON-ZERO, PLAUSIBLE test count rather than a green exit — "Ran 0 tests" is the single most common false green in this repo, and it has now appeared via (a) a bare `clojure -M:test -n <ns>` from implementation/, (b) a CLJS runner selecting no namespace after a rename, and (c) a map fixture swallowing the whole body.

ALSO FROM #6415, worth copying: it proved its own hydration harness by feeding it KNOWN-BAD HTML first, and a separate non-vacuity assertion then caught its OWN first version rendering an empty client tree and passing. Two independent controls on the harness before trusting any result from it.
AND: reset-failed-boundaries! is now the FIFTH process-global defonce table keyed outside app-db (with request-slots, response-slots, pending-error-traces, installed-payloads). Any test that touches one MUST reset it or it leaks into siblings — #6389 CI failure was exactly that.

THE API-MANIFEST LANE IS SEVEN CO-EDITED FILES, NOT FIVE — and the two extra are NON-VACUITY ANCHORS that spell the surface as a LITERAL NAME SET. Found 2026-07-24 by the rf2-drpa3.121 worker (PR #6772) while adding t/with-render.

THE FIVE EVERYONE KNOWS: the facade block; spec/api-manifest.edn (REGENERATED); spec/api-manifest-metadata.edn (classification row); spec/API.md (roster row); docs/api/<ns>.md (member heading).

THE TWO THAT BITE:
  6. implementation/scripts/api-manifest/probe/test/.../cljs_manifest_probe_cljs_test.cljs
  7. implementation/scripts/api-manifest/test/.../freehand_test_enrolment_test.clj
Both hard-code the surface as a literal list of names, so adding a public var makes them WRONG.

⚠️ THE ASYMMETRY IS THE DANGEROUS PART: only the JVM one (7) FAILS LOUDLY. The CLJS one (6) was caught only by READING — the worker spotted it before it ran. So a worker that adds a verb, sees the JVM anchor red, fixes it, and goes green has NOT necessarily fixed both. CHECK BOTH BY READING, do not rely on a red to find them.

The JVM anchor also asserted a SINGLE :kind for all rows, which breaks the moment the surface gains a member of a different kind. The fix made it stricter rather than looser: pin each NAME against its DERIVED :kind (here five :fn and one :macro) instead of asserting one kind for the set.

GENERAL FORM, and this is why it is worth remembering beyond this lane: A NON-VACUITY ANCHOR THAT ENUMERATES A SURFACE IS A MAINTENANCE COUPLING. It exists to stop the gate passing on an empty set, which is right — but it converts every addition to that surface into an edit of the test. When you write one, prefer deriving the expected set from the same source the gate reads, or at minimum make it fail LOUDLY on both hosts. An anchor that silently tolerates drift on one host is worse than none, because it teaches you the surface is covered when it is half-covered.

ALSO CONFIRMED ON THIS LANE (unchanged, still true): the rebase trap. git AUTO-MERGES the generated spec/api-manifest.edn with no conflict markers and leaves a STALE :var-count, and the resulting drift error reads like a formatting or toolchain problem. Cure is plain gen, then --check exit 0, AND an EMPTY git diff on that file. The empty-diff step is the one people skip and the only one that proves the committed file equals the generator output.

EDITING A CRLF-STORED FILE UNDER core.autocrlf=true SILENTLY NORMALISES THE WHOLE FILE TO LF — a multi-thousand-line whitespace diff that reads as real content. Found 2026-07-24 by the rf2-drpa3.103 worker, which caught it before committing.

THE CASE: spec/011-SSR.md is stored on main with CRLF. A normal edit produced a ~4,200-line diff on a HOT-ZONE file for a change that should have been +45 lines. Nothing warned; the diff simply looked enormous.

THE CURE the worker used: rebuild the file BYTE-EXACTLY from its base blob plus the intended change, then re-add with `git -c core.autocrlf=false add <file>`. Committed diff came out at +45 insertions and nothing else.

THE CHECK, and it is cheap: after ANY edit to a tracked file, run `git diff --numstat` and confirm the line counts match what you intended. A diff far larger than your change is a line-ending normalisation, not your edit.

⚠️ THIS COMPOUNDS WITH THE HOT-ZONE RULE. spec/ files are sequential-never-parallel precisely because they collide; a whole-file normalisation guarantees a conflict with every other branch touching that file, and buries the real change so a reviewer cannot see it. On a hot-zone file the damage is not cosmetic.

RELATED, ALREADY RECORDED: `sed -i` on a tracked file does the same thing for the same reason on this Windows checkout — which is why briefs forbid it and require the Edit tool. This is the SAME hazard reached through an ordinary edit rather than through sed, so the sed ban alone does not cover it. Put the numstat check in briefs that touch spec/ files, not just the sed ban.

MAYOR NOTE: my briefs already say "no sed -i" and "check git diff --numstat shows only the lines you intended" — the second half turned out to be the load-bearing one, and I had been treating it as a footnote to the first.
